On the night Ramchandra escapes, Udayaditya is free and in command: he orders Sitaram to open the locked door, draws his sword, and—because Sitaram will not fight the man who twice saved his life—disarms him and binds him head to foot, leaving the guard lying there while the prince walks away. On the night of Udayaditya’s own escape the roles reverse: he is the helpless prisoner, and Sitaram throws open the cell, seizes him, and nearly carries him out. In the open field Udayaditya asks Sitaram where to go, and Sitaram leads him.

The song voices an old man’s grief at being left with emptiness: those who were once his no longer answer, nothing of “mine” remains, and he has no spirit to go on living. Basanta Ray first hums it alone in Raigarh at sunset, before the news, as a quiet lament that those he sang for and longed to embrace are gone. He sings it again in Jessore, slowly, holding Vibha’s hand before Surma’s empty, silent room, after the household’s joy has collapsed into desolation.

Pratapaditya received Ramchandra with cold, unceremonious slight: a late, scant welcome, no joy or haste, interrupted talk of floods, and a casual dismissal to the inner quarters while he attended business, so Ramchandra felt deliberately insulted and saw his father-in-law’s superiority. Later, in his own court, Ramchandra reverses that hierarchy. He smiles while courtiers daily degrade Pratapaditya’s short lineage—as earthworm, leech, and snake—claim his ancestor was anointed by Ramchandra’s grandfather’s little toe, punish anyone who compares them, and treat the marriage itself as a condescension that would lower his house if Vibha were brought home.

She leaves Raigarh, takes the name Mangala, and settles on the outskirts of Jessore, befriending the palace servants and tracking every scrap of news while performing rites for the deaths of Pratapaditya and Surma. When the Rajmahishi sends Matangini to her for a secret medicine to win Udayaditya’s heart from Surma, Mangala grinds roots and chants mantras for five nights and prepares a poison meant so that he will feel no pity when Surma dies. Surma then dies of poison—the palace believing she took it by her own hand—and afterward Mangala enters his dark bedchamber in a storm, demands his love, and takes the ring from his finger.

Udayaditya first wishes he had never been born crown prince or sole heir, sure he lacks the intellect to rule. At sixteen, Hosenkhali falls into disorder under him; the court takes the subjects’ love as proof he can never govern, and his father despises him, likening him to Basanta Ray. He endures the neglect and longs to leave with Surma, yet stays for her. Brought later before Pratapaditya as a prisoner and told he is unworthy of the kingdom, he agrees and begs release from the throne. That day, touching Ma-Kali’s feet before his father, he swears he will never accept even an iota of Jessore, never sit on its throne or touch its scepter, names Samaraditya heir, and leaves for Kashi as an ascetic.

When forced to leave Udayaditya, Basanta Ray seizes his sitar and plays it furiously, but tears blur his eyes and choke him until he must stop and set it down. He leaves the instrument behind and vows never to play it again, abandoning the companion of his joy with the grandson he is losing. Later, alone, that eternal companion is gone. Asked why he no longer plays, he says the sitar is still there, only its strings have broken and it can no longer be tuned. Song still rises, yet there is no joy in it, for those he sang for no longer answer. The sitar’s silencing—from frantic, failed playing, to renunciation, to broken untunable strings—mirrors how separation from Udayaditya has emptied his spirit, until news of the imprisonment brings his world crashing down.

Earlier, after his marriage, Udayaditya was known for going out as he pleased, involving himself in the subjects’ affairs, and acting against the king’s wishes. He fought oppression with all his might, treated danger as a trifle, and would stop an official and protect a subject without considering the consequences. After Surma’s death that courage is gone. A blind fear of Pratapaditya seizes him, and he hesitates in every matter. Told of a planned night raid and burning, he has his horse readied and then sends it away. Seeing an official beat a bound subject who begs for mercy, he cannot bear the sight and runs into the house. When stipends are stopped, he thinks of sending money, then hesitates, and never sends it.

In Jessore she is dressed as a royal bride for his arrival: eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring, and an elaborate coiffure, her shy face radiant with joy. After Surma's death, the bedchamber window is a place of absence and memory: he leaves empty the spot where she used to sit and looks out on the same moonlight, garden, and breeze, hoping she will somehow be there, so the unchanged view only deepens his grief. In the prison, the small window becomes the opposite of confinement. Through it he watches the sky and the birds and believes his own cage will one day break; that narrow patch of view is the only place he feels naturally free, beyond any king's power, while moving away from it leaves him in darkness and makes him forget liberation.

Sitaram, penniless, courts the moneylender Rukmini with extravagant flirtation so she will lend without pressing for interest or repayment. She plays along, treating the loan as affection, while he never pays and they begin to scheme in secret. When Udayaditya is imprisoned, that pose collapses: Sitaram storms in, curses her, nearly strikes her, and threatens to burn her house, grind her face on the floor, smear her with lime and soot, and drive her from the city unless he frees the prince. Her answering hatred is possessive—she claims the Yubaraj as hers alone. Later, believing her dead, Sitaram comes to rob her cottage and finds her alive, wet and shivering, returned from Yama’s door. His mockery and renewed fake endearments drive her to fetch a curved blade and vow to burn him and the prince and anoint herself with their ashes. He flees as she strikes the floor where he stood.

The guardhouse fire begins as a diversion. Sitaram’s men set several guard huts ablaze at once and sabotage the firefighting, so the guards abandon Udayaditya’s door to save their belongings. Under cover of that chaos, Sitaram pulls him from the prison on the pretext that it too is burning and spirits him away.

It then becomes a staged death. While attention stays on the huts, his men set the empty cell alight. Sitaram throws in bones, a skull, and the prince’s sword. False reports follow: the prince was seen at the window, heard screaming, then silent after the roof collapsed. The court accepts the burnt sword and these accounts as proof he died in the fire, concealing the escape.

Pratapaditya first scorns the Emperor of Delhi, forbidding even his name and, when told a complaint has already been lodged against him there, declaring himself the Emperor’s judge. That dismissed threat is later turned on his son. Bhagavat and Sitaram forge a petition in the crown prince’s name, sealed with his own seal, written as if Udayaditya were accusing his father of treason before the Emperor to seize the kingdom. Bhagavat does not send it to Delhi. He brings it to Pratapaditya as a petition seized from the prince’s servant on the way to the Emperor, so the false appeal becomes the charge by which the father condemns his son.

While Surma is present, Vibha secretly has her style the hair the Mahishi has made unbearable, so the coiffure marks Surma’s intimate care against the palace’s heavy adornment. After Surma is gone, Vibha still sits at braiding time waiting for her to come; evening and night fall, and the hair stays unbraided.
